rules.rule: a record that declares a privacy mode must declare one of the modes in privacy.modes

a ref that begins with privacy.reserved_prefix is a privacy declaration and must be exactly the anonymous ref; a hand-written ref that only resembles one is a malformed declaration and the snapshot is refused

any other external_ref value is application payload and is NOT a privacy declaration - it neither masks nor unmaskes anything. The live ledger carries 'genesis', 'hosted-liveness-proof' and 'onenness-tor-mainnet:buy:<id>', and a rule that forbade them would reject the chain it is protecting
rules.on_violation: nothing to enforce: the ref is ignored here

rules.rule: the privacy field and external_ref must agree - a record that says 'anonymous' in one and 'public' in the other is a tampered record, not a typo
a chain record may never store the anonymous label as its 'from' address: the ledger debits the signer, so a stored label is either a lost address or a lie
every public projection of a record must mask 'from' when the record is anonymous
rules.on_violation: a page would publish an address the sender hid

rules.rule: a peer's snapshot must arrive with the policy it implements, and that policy's signature must verify against a locally pinned key
a peer's policy hash must equal a hash this node already trusts; a node with different privacy rules cannot sync, in either direction
every record in a snapshot is re-checked against privacy.* before import, not just the blocks

peer_sync.hash_algorithm: sha3-256 over canonical JSON of this document
peer_sync.offline: verification never uses the network: an unreachable origin cannot change or block a local decision

not_claimed: This is not a zero-knowledge proof system and does not claim to be. The chain is a transparent-account ledger: balances are public, so an anonymous transfer masks the sender's address on the record, it does not make the transfer untraceable (see privacy.py).

No auditor has reviewed this policy. It is a machine-checkable statement of the rules the code already enforces - calling that 'audited' would be a lie, and the signature proves provenance (which key signed it), not correctness.
A node can run modified code and still hold a valid key. The gate stops modified nodes from syncing *data*, which is the only thing a remote verifier can actually decide.
